Cannabis 101

Dry January With Cannabis: A Practical Guide to Going California Sober

Thinking of trading drinks for low-dose cannabis this January? Here is what California sober means, who should check with a professional first and how to pace the month.

By the High Society teamPublished October 24, 20268 min read

08min readCannabis 101
In this article
  1. What California sober means, and what it doesn't
  2. Talk to a professional first if this applies to you
  3. Replacing the after-work drink
  4. Protecting your mornings
  5. Sleep and evenings: what research says
  6. Social plans without alcohol
  7. Setting limits and keeping track
  8. Dry January cannabis formats, side by side
  9. Sticking with it for all 31 days
  10. Frequently asked questions

Key takeaways

  • California sober usually means skipping alcohol while still using cannabis. It is not a recovery method.
  • If you drink heavily or are in recovery, talk with a doctor or counselor before you change anything.
  • Research on swapping cannabis for alcohol is mixed: some studies find substitution, others find people use both.
  • Michigan caps THC drinks at 10 mg per serving, and smaller doses taken earlier help protect your mornings.
  • Never combine cannabis with alcohol, and never drive after using it.

A dry January cannabis plan usually means skipping alcohol for the month and, for some adults, reaching for a low-dose THC drink or edible instead. Many people call that approach California sober. It can be a useful sober-curious experiment, but it isn't a recovery method, and it isn't right for everyone. Here's what to know before you start, plus practical ways to replace the after-work drink, protect your mornings and keep the month on track.

What California sober means, and what it doesn't

Dry January is a month off from drinking, and the sober-curious idea builds on it: taking a hard look at how much alcohol fits your life, without necessarily quitting for good. California sober is one version of that. It usually describes skipping alcohol while still using cannabis, though people use the term loosely, and some include other substances.

What it isn't: a recovery program, a fix for a drinking problem or a promise that you'll feel better. Researchers have asked for more than two decades whether people actually use cannabis instead of alcohol, and the answers vary. A 2020 systematic review of 65 studies found 30 that pointed to substitution, 17 in which people used both together, 14 that showed neither and 4 that showed both. The authors called the evidence mixed and said study quality varied.

Talk to a professional first if this applies to you

Some people should check with a doctor, counselor or treatment provider before making any change this month:

  • You drink heavily or every day. Stopping suddenly after heavy, regular drinking can cause alcohol withdrawal. Symptoms often start within 8 hours of the last drink, and severe withdrawal can bring seizures or delirium tremens, which can be fatal.
  • You're in recovery, or you think you may have an alcohol use disorder. Talk with your counselor, sponsor or treatment provider before adding cannabis to the picture.
  • You're pregnant or breastfeeding. The CDC warns that cannabis use during pregnancy or breastfeeding may harm the baby.
  • You take medicines or manage a health condition. A clinician can tell you how cannabis might fit with your care.

For free, confidential help finding treatment or support, call SAMHSA's National Helpline at 1-800-662-HELP (4357). It answers 24 hours a day, every day of the year, in English and Spanish. It's a referral and information line; if you're in crisis, call or text 988.

Replacing the after-work drink

The after-work drink is often about the ritual: the glass, the pause, the shift into evening. You can keep most of that, whether or not you try THC drinks instead of alcohol.

  • Start alcohol-free and THC-free. Sparkling water with citrus, a good tea or a mocktail covers the ritual on its own. Our guide to cannabis mocktails shows how to build infused versions with a measured dose per glass.
  • Try a low-dose THC drink. In Michigan, a THC beverage can hold no more than 10 mg of THC per serving and 100 mg per container. Starting well below a full serving is the cautious choice.
  • Pace it like an edible. A THC drink is swallowed, and the CDC notes that you may not feel an edible or a drink for as long as two hours. Sip slowly, then wait before having more.

THC drinks don't work like beer or wine. They're measured in milligrams, not glasses, and the effects build slowly. Our guide to THC-infused drinks and our comparison of drink and edible timing go deeper.

Protecting your mornings

Clearer mornings are a big part of why people try Dry January. A few habits help keep them that way:

  • Start low. A small dose is easier to manage.
  • Go earlier. A drink or edible may need as long as two hours to come on, so a late serving can still be building when you head to bed. Moving it earlier gives it time to play out.
  • Use one format at a time. Pairing a drink with a vape makes it hard to tell what's affecting you.
  • Plan around early starts. If you'll drive, work a demanding shift or need to be fully alert in the morning, take the night off.

Sleep and evenings: what research says

Some people reach for cannabis at night hoping to sleep better. The research is thinner than the enthusiasm. A 2019 review of clinical studies found that many reported better sleep. It also flagged real limits: small samples, sleep often treated as a side question in studies of people with other health conditions, and relatively few validated sleep measures.

So be cautious about sleep claims, and pay attention to how your own nights go. If you use cannabis in the evening, keep the dose low and keep some nights cannabis-free. If poor sleep is a long-running problem, talk with a clinician.

Social plans without alcohol

January still brings birthdays, game nights and dinners out. A few ways to stay social:

  • Bring your own drink. An alcohol-free option you enjoy means you're never empty-handed.
  • Suggest daytime plans. Brunch, a winter walk or a movie takes the focus off drinking.
  • Keep cannabis private. Use it at home or at a private gathering where the host is comfortable with it, never in public or in a car.
  • Don't mix. The CDC says using alcohol and cannabis at the same time is likely to cause more impairment than either one alone. If friends are drinking, keep your own cannabis use low or skip it.
  • Plan the ride home. Never drive after using cannabis.

Setting limits and keeping track

A month is long enough to slide into a nightly habit you didn't plan. Set your limits before January 1:

  • How many days a week you'll use cannabis, if any
  • A top dose per session, in milligrams
  • A cutoff time each evening
  • Several cannabis-free days each week

Then keep a simple log:

DateWhat and how muchTimeHow the next morning felt
Jan. 3THC drink, 2.5 mg6:30 p.m.Clear
Jan. 5NoneNoneClear

If you notice you're using more than you planned, or that skipping a day feels hard, bring it up with a clinician.

Dry January cannabis formats, side by side

If you decide to include cannabis this month, keep the lineup small. These are the formats people often consider, with what to know about each:

FormatMichigan limitTimingGood to know
THC drinks10 mg THC per serving, 100 mg per containerYou may not feel it for two hoursCheck the servings per can or bottle
Low-dose edibles10 mg THC per servingSlow; allow two hoursSmall pieces make low doses easy
Tinctures10 mg THC per dose for adult useDrops you swallow work on an edible's scheduleA marked dropper measures small amounts
CBD-forward productsSame per-serving limits apply to the THCVaries by formatLess THC, but check the THC figure

Start with one format and the smallest practical dose. Our guide to microdosing THC and CBD covers low-dose routines in detail.

Sticking with it for all 31 days

These Dry January tips help the month hold up past the first week:

  • Write down your reason. Better mornings, saving money or plain curiosity: keep it somewhere you'll see it.
  • Tell a friend. Someone checking in makes the month easier.
  • Plan for the hard moments. Fridays, birthdays and big games are easier with a plan and a drink you like.
  • Don't let one slip end the month. Start again the next day.
  • Review at the end. Look back at your log. Did your sleep, mornings or spending change? Use what you learned to decide what February looks like.

Our guide to cannabis and New Year's resolutions has more ideas for goals you'll keep. Cannabis is for adults 21 and older. Please consume responsibly.

Frequently asked questions

What does California sober mean?

It usually means avoiding alcohol while still using cannabis, though people use the term loosely and some include other substances. It's a lifestyle label, not a recovery program or medical advice. If you're in recovery from alcohol or any other substance, talk with your treatment provider before adding cannabis to your plans.

Is cannabis a good alternative to alcohol for Dry January?

It depends on you. Research on swapping cannabis for alcohol is mixed: a 2020 review of 65 studies found evidence of substitution in some and of people using both in others. Cannabis has its own risks, including impairment that makes driving unsafe. If you try it, keep doses low, track your use and never combine the two.

Are THC drinks like alcohol?

Not really. A THC drink is measured in milligrams, not standard drinks, and your body handles it like an edible, so you may not feel it for as long as two hours. In Michigan, a THC drink can hold up to 10 mg per serving and 100 mg per container. Sip one serving slowly, wait, and never mix it with alcohol.

Can I do Dry January with cannabis if I'm in recovery?

Talk with your counselor, sponsor or treatment provider first. California sober isn't a recovery method, and only you and the people supporting you can judge whether cannabis fits your plan. For free, confidential help any time, call SAMHSA's National Helpline at 1-800-662-HELP (4357). It's open 24 hours a day, every day.

Sources

  1. Risso C. et al., Does cannabis complement or substitute alcohol consumption? A systematic review of human and animal studies, Journal of Psychopharmacology (2020)pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov
  2. MedlinePlus (National Library of Medicine): Alcohol withdrawalmedlineplus.gov
  3. Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration: SAMHSA's National Helplinesamhsa.gov
  4. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention: Cannabis frequently asked questionscdc.gov
  5. Kuhathasan N. et al., The use of cannabinoids for sleep: a critical review on clinical trials, Experimental and Clinical Psychopharmacology (2019)pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov
  6. Michigan Cannabis Regulatory Agency: Maximum THC Concentrations for Marijuana-Infused Products (technical bulletin, April 2025)michigan.gov
21+

For adults 21 and older. Keep cannabis away from children and pets, and never drive after consuming. Michigan law does not allow cannabis use in public places.
